core_obligations: Show that the projection from the base change of the target to the target is open, using that the field extension is universally open (proof lines 5869-5872).
Deduce the forward implication from the preservation of dominance under open base change (proof lines 5873-5875).
For the converse, note that the same projection is surjective, so the composite of the base changed morphism with it is dominant (proof lines 5876-5879).
Identify that composite with the composite of the projection to the source with the original morphism, and conclude that the original morphism is dominant (proof lines 5879-5880).
proof_roadmap: Openness of the base change of the target (proof lines 5869-5872).
Forward direction by open base change (proof lines 5873-5875).
Converse direction by surjectivity and compositeness (proof lines 5876-5880).
difficulty_reason: For a field extension E over k, the lemma asserts that a morphism over k is dominant if and only if its pullback to the base change to E is dominant (statement lines 5861-5866). The proof splits the equivalence. For the forward direction it uses that the morphism from the spectrum of E to the spectrum of k is universally open, so the projection from the base change of the target to the target is open, and then a cited lemma gives that dominant morphisms are preserved by open base change (proof lines 5869-5875). For the converse it uses that the same projection is surjective, so composing the dominance of the base changed morphism with it gives dominance of the composite, which is also the composite of the projection to the source with the original morphism, whence the original morphism is dominant (proof lines 5876-5880). The claim is H2: the two directions rest on different properties of the field extension -- openness in one and surjectivity in the other -- and both are used explicitly, with a short compositeness argument at the end.
